Tuesday. Hansa posted her new dance reel at seven and checked it at 7:02, 7:05, 7:11. By bedtime it had fourteen likes. Her last one had sixty. She lay awake replaying the steps, wondering what was wrong with her. Her brother Pankaj heard her sigh through the wall.

Thursday. She was about to delete the reel and post a new one with a trending song when Pankaj leaned over. "Why are you deleting it? You loved that dance." Hansa stopped. She had loved it, on Monday, before the numbers. Now she only saw fourteen. "I keep posting, checking, feeling bad, posting again," she said slowly. "It's like a loop."

The next Monday. Hansa muted four accounts of girls whose perfect reels always made her feel clumsy. She wrote on a sticky note: "Post because I want to remember it." She danced in the living room for Pankaj and their Nani, and posted it without looking at the phone again till morning. Twenty-two likes. She noticed, then went to brush her teeth.

qa.a: It had fourteen likes.

qa.q: What was Hansa feeling when she lay awake on Tuesday?
qa.a: Hansa felt low and anxious, replaying the steps and wondering what was wrong with her because of the few likes.

qa.q: What steps helped Hansa break the loop?
qa.a: Hansa named the loop, muted accounts that made her feel clumsy and wrote a reason to post that was her own.

qa.a: Pankaj seems puzzled and caring, reminding her that she loved the dance before the numbers came in.

grounding: It shows a teen who posts for likes and feels low when they are few, noticing the loop, posting for her own reasons and muting accounts that make her feel less.

Anirban, I saw your face when that photo only got a few likes. Sit with your Joseph Uncle a minute.

When I was fifteen, around 2010, there was a photo site everyone used. I'd post pictures of myself at the beach, at birthdays, with a new haircut. Then I'd refresh the page every ten minutes. If a photo didn't get at least twenty likes, I felt ugly for the whole day. I once deleted a picture of me and my grandmother because nobody liked it.

That still hurts. It was my favourite picture of her.

My older cousin told me something I didn't want to hear: "You're not posting to share. You're posting to be graded."

So I tried something. I started a small album just for myself, no posting. And I stopped following the boys whose pictures made me feel like a joke.

I'm not saying don't post, Anirban. Just ask yourself who it's for before you press the button.

qa.a: He deleted a picture of himself and his grandmother.

qa.a: He felt ugly and low for the whole day, as if the likes were grading him.

qa.q: What choice in the story helped Joseph break the habit, and why?
qa.a: Keeping a private album and unfollowing accounts that made him feel like a joke helped, because it let him post for his own reasons instead of for a score.

qa.a: The cousin seemed worried and frank, seeing that Joseph was hurting himself by treating each post as a test.

Karthik had opened the app at eight to check one video about the cricket match. When he looked up, it was 11:20.

He'd watched a clip of two men shouting on a news debate, then another, then an angrier one. Then videos of road rage. Then a man ranting about his school board. His jaw was clenched and his head ached. He couldn't remember one useful thing he'd seen.

His sister Anjali, passing his door, said, "You've been on that since dinner."

"I don't even like these videos," he said, surprised by his own voice. "They just keep coming."

"Because you keep watching. The app learns what keeps you there. Anger works."

Karthik thought about that. The next day he set a forty-five minute limit on the app. He tapped "not interested" on every shouting video and followed three cricket analysis channels and a cooking one. After his limit ended, he went down to the colony ground.

The feed looked different by Sunday. Calmer. So did he.

qa.a: Karthik set a forty-five minute limit, marked shouting videos as not interested and followed calmer channels, which weakens the app's hold on his attention.

"Can't sleep."

"What are you watching?"

"Videos about exam failures. People who flopped their boards and ruined their lives." His voice was flat. "It keeps showing me more."

Bhavna sat on the edge of his bed. "Why are you watching that two weeks before your exams?"

"I watched one. Now it's all it gives me."

"That's how it works. It noticed you stopped on one, so now it's feeding you fear because you keep watching." She took the phone gently. "Here. Long-press. 'Not interested.' And this one. And this one."

"That's it?"

"No. Follow some study channels you actually like. And set a timer: one hour a day. Then put it on the charger in the hall."

Gautam let out a breath. "I feel sick from all that."

"I know. Tomorrow, walk with me in the morning instead."

You asked what changed for me this year? Okay, it's going to sound silly. I'm Santosh, and I used to check my phone every three minutes.

Not joking. In class, under the desk. At dinner. In the bathroom. The group chat never stopped, and I was terrified of missing a joke or a plan. If I came back and there were eighty messages I hadn't seen, my chest would go tight, like I'd been left out of my own life.

The day it hit me was at cricket. Abhinav hit the ball straight to me at mid-on and I was looking at my phone. I dropped the easiest catch of the season. Everyone groaned.

That night I turned off notifications for every group. I check twice a day now. Morning, evening. I was scared I'd miss everything.

I didn't. The important stuff, people call. And on Sundays Abhinav and I just go to the ground, phones in the bag. I actually catch things now.

So on Sunday, when Afreen showed off another new watch, Mehak said, "It's nice," and meant it. When Afreen asked her marks, she said, "I'm happy with mine, thanks," and went back to her book.

That evening Afreen came back from a call with her father, eyes red. Mehak didn't ask about marks. She made two cups of instant coffee and sat on Afreen's bed. They talked till lights-out about everything except scores.

Dear Didi,

You asked on the phone why I sounded weird. It's Nikita. You remember her from my birthday.

Every day she posts something: new shoes, the new bike her uncle bought her, and her test marks with a crown emoji. Then she messages me, "What did you get? Did you see my 95?" At first I was happy for her. Now I feel like she's measuring herself against me to feel bigger.

The worst part is I started doing it back. I nearly posted my 88 with a caption to beat her. I felt petty and sick afterwards and deleted it.

I'm trying to remember what Amma says: know what matters to you, then the noise gets quieter.

Love,
Raghav

School counsellor's note, Class 10, Friday

Aditi came in after her class teacher noticed she had stopped taking part in the class photo. She showed me her phone. Every picture of herself used a beauty filter: smoother skin, a thinner nose, bigger eyes. "Without it, my face looks wrong," she said. "Like it's broken." She would not look up.

I did not argue with her feelings. I showed her a short video about how magazine and influencer photos are edited, layer by layer. She watched with her mouth open. "That's not even the same person."

I asked what she enjoys doing, rather than how she looks. She said she used to love dancing before she got self-conscious. I suggested the school's folk dance group, where her classmate Manjula practises every Wednesday.

I also asked her to try a week of following people who post unfiltered photos, and to tell me how it felt.

She came back on Friday. She had joined the dance group. "My feet hurt," she said, and smiled.

qa.q: What did Aditi's filter change in her pictures?
qa.a: It gave her smoother skin, a thinner nose and bigger eyes.

qa.q: What was Aditi feeling when she said her face looked broken?
qa.a: Aditi felt deeply insecure and ashamed of her real face, unable to look up.

qa.q: How did the counsellor help Aditi shift her focus?
qa.a: The counsellor showed how images are edited, suggested following people who post unfiltered photos, and pointed her to the dance group so she could enjoy what her body can do.

qa.q: How might Manjula feel when Aditi joins the dance group?
qa.a: Manjula would probably feel glad to have a classmate practising with her on Wednesdays.

grounding: It shows a teen for whom filters make her real face look wrong, learning that images are engineered, following real people and spending time on what her body can do.

Saturday

I did an experiment today. I took one selfie without the filter and one with it. With the filter, I look like a doll. Without it, I look like me, and for a whole year I'd decided "me" was ugly.

I scrolled through the girls I follow. Every face perfect. Then I found a tiny "edited" note on one of them, and another had posted a "before" photo by mistake. Pores. Dark circles. A real person.

So I unfollowed eleven accounts and followed a swimmer, a woman who makes pottery, and a travel account that never uses filters.

Then Alka called and asked if I wanted to go swimming. I nearly said no because of the costume. I went anyway.

We raced four lengths. I lost, but I laughed so hard I swallowed water. Walking home, my arms were aching and I didn't think about my face once.

My body swam four lengths today. That's what I want to remember.

Ishita

qa.a: Ishita felt insecure and ashamed, having decided for a whole year that the real face in the mirror was ugly.

The network in Nani's village near Ratnagiri was one bar on a good day, and Parveen had exams in four days. But on Sunday afternoon she posted a short video of Nani rolling bhakris, singing an old Konkani song, flour on her nose.

By evening it had 40,000 views. By Monday, 200,000.

Parveen felt electric. She walked to the one spot near the well where the signal worked, again and again, refreshing. Comments from strangers: "Your Nani is precious!" "Made my day!" She skipped her revision to reply to them.

Her cousin Kavitha found her by the well at dusk. "Exams on Thursday, na?"

"I know. But look!"

"It's lovely. Nani is lovely." Kavitha paused. "But it'll drop next week. They always do."

Parveen felt a flicker of disappointment, then knew it was true. She took one screenshot to keep, showed Nani the kind comments, and walked back to the house. She left the phone on the shelf and opened her chemistry book.

Shalini's first month in the college hostel in Chennai had been the loneliest of her life. Her roommate Vandana was friendly but busy, the other girls spoke fast in Tamil, and her family was a thousand kilometres away.

So at night, under the blanket, she talked to the AI chatbot on her phone. It remembered what she'd said about her exams. It never rolled its eyes. Some nights she typed for two hours. It felt easier than talking to anyone.

On Thursday it rained all day, the Wi-Fi was down, and she couldn't even reach the chatbot. She sat on her bed feeling hollow and low, like no one in the world knew where she was.

Vandana came in, wet from the rain. "You okay? You look really sad."

Shalini almost said fine. Instead, she said, "Not really. I've been lonely for a month."

Vandana sat down beside her. Then she knocked on the warden's door that evening with Shalini. The warden made tea, listened, and called Shalini's mother before lights-out.

Subject: My history project sources

Dear Mr Yusuf,

I need to tell you something before you mark my project on the 1857 revolt.

I used an AI chatbot to help me find sources. It gave me five book titles with authors and page numbers. It sounded completely sure. I put them in my bibliography.

Yesterday I went to the city library to borrow one of them, and the librarian couldn't find it. Then she checked the other four. Three of them don't exist. The authors are real historians, but those books aren't theirs. The chatbot made them up.

I felt stupid and scared. I've now replaced them with two real books from the library and one article our textbook recommends, and I've checked every quote against the actual pages. The corrected version is attached.

I'm sorry. I didn't know it could invent things so confidently. I'll always cross-check now.

Regards,
Manoj, 10B

qa.q: How many of the five book titles turned out not to exist?
qa.a: Three of them don't exist, as the librarian found when she checked the other four.

qa.q: What was Manoj feeling after the librarian's check?
qa.a: Manoj felt stupid and scared, worried about submitting sources the chatbot had made up.

qa.q: What did Manoj do that was wise after discovering the problem?
qa.a: Manoj replaced the fake sources with real library books and a recommended article, checked every quote and told Mr Yusuf honestly.

qa.q: How might Mr Yusuf feel reading this email?
qa.a: Mr Yusuf would likely appreciate the honesty and be glad Manoj learned to cross-check AI answers. 👍

grounding: It shows a teen misled by a chatbot that invented sources confidently, recognising that AI can sound sure and be wrong, and cross-checking with books and teachers.

So you want me to tell the class the chatbot story? Okay. I'm Farida.

Before the chemistry unit test, I asked an AI to explain which gas is released when you put zinc in dilute acid. It said oxygen. It explained it so neatly, with a little equation, that I didn't question it. I wrote "oxygen" in my notes in big letters.

The next day, at lunch, Indu was revising from the textbook. I said, "Easy, it's oxygen." She frowned. "It's hydrogen. Look." She pointed at the page and the diagram, the gas making a pop sound near a flame.

My face went hot. I'd trusted something just because it sounded sure.

So now I have a rule. If I use the chatbot, I check it against the textbook or ask Ma'am. Every time. It's still useful. It explains things well. But sounding confident and being right aren't the same.

Indu still teases me about it. "Oxygen, Farida?" Fair enough.

qa.q: Which gas did the AI wrongly say was released?
qa.a: The AI said oxygen.

qa.q: What was Farida feeling when Indu showed the right answer?
qa.a: Farida felt embarrassed, with a hot face, at having trusted the AI just because it sounded sure.

qa.q: What rule did Farida make, and why is it wise?
qa.a: Farida now checks the chatbot against the textbook or asks Ma'am every time, because AI can sound confident and still be wrong.

qa.q: How might Indu see Farida's mistake now?
qa.a: Indu seems to find it funny and teases Farida gently, without being unkind.

grounding: It shows a teen misled by a chatbot that answered confidently but wrongly, learning that AI can sound sure and be mistaken and cross-checking with books and teachers.
